questions.q: Two lines with slopes $m_1$ and $m_2$ are perpendicular when:
questions.solution:
Perpendicular lines satisfy $\mathbf{m_1m_2 = -1}$, that is each slope is the negative reciprocal of the other.

The one exception is a vertical and a horizontal line, where one slope is undefined and the product cannot be formed.

Parallel lines have $m_1 = m_2$.

questions.q: The centre of the circle $x^{2} + y^{2} - 4x + 6y - 3 = 0$ is:
questions.solution:
For $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c = 0$, the centre is $(-g, -f)$.

Here $2g = -4$ so $g = -2$, and $2f = 6$ so $f = 3$.

Centre $= (-g, -f) = \mathbf{(2, -3)}$.

The radius is $\sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}-c} = \sqrt{4+9+3} = 4$.

questions.q: Two non-zero vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are perpendicular when:
questions.solution:
$\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$.

For non-zero vectors this vanishes exactly when $\cos\theta = 0$, that is $\theta = 90^\circ$. So $\mathbf{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0}$.

The **cross** product vanishing means the opposite: $\sin\theta = 0$, so the vectors are **parallel**.

questions.q: The eccentricity of a parabola is:
questions.solution:
Eccentricity classifies the conic sections:

circle $e = 0$, ellipse $0 < e < 1$, **parabola $e = 1$**, hyperbola $e > 1$.

$e = 1$ means every point is **equidistant** from the focus and the directrix, which is the defining property of a parabola.

questions.q: The distance between the points $(1,2,3)$ and $(4,6,3)$ is:
questions.solution:
$d = \sqrt{(4-1)^{2} + (6-2)^{2} + (3-3)^{2}}$

$= \sqrt{9 + 16 + 0} = \sqrt{25} = \mathbf{5}$.

The $z$-coordinates are equal, so this reduces to a 3-4-5 triangle in a plane parallel to the $xy$-plane.

options: The area of the triangle formed
The area of the parallelogram with sides $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$
questions.solution:
$|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}| = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta$, which is exactly base times perpendicular height — the **area of the parallelogram** spanned by the two vectors.

The **triangle** on the same two vectors is half of that, $\tfrac12|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|$.

The scalar triple product $|\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})|$ gives the volume of the parallelepiped.

questions.q: The distance of the point $(x_1,y_1)$ from the line $Ax+By+C=0$ is:
questions.solution:
$d = \mathbf{\dfrac{|Ax_1+By_1+C|}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}}}$.

The modulus is needed because distance is non-negative; without it the sign tells you which **side** of the line the point lies on, which is itself useful.

Setting $d = 0$ recovers the condition that the point lies on the line.

questions.q: The direction cosines $l$, $m$, $n$ of a line satisfy:
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2} = 1}$.

The direction cosines are the components of a **unit** vector along the line, so the sum of their squares is 1 by Pythagoras in three dimensions.

Direction **ratios** $a$, $b$, $c$ are any proportional set and need not satisfy this; dividing them by $\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}$ turns them into direction cosines.

questions.q: For the ellipse $\dfrac{x^{2}}{25} + \dfrac{y^{2}}{9} = 1$, the length of the major axis is:
questions.solution:
Comparing with $\dfrac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$: $a^{2}=25$ so $a=5$, and $b^{2}=9$ so $b=3$.

Since $a > b$ the major axis is along $x$, and its **length** is $2a = \mathbf{10}$.

The common error is answering 5, which is the semi-major axis. The minor axis has length $2b = 6$.

questions.q: Find the slope of the line joining $(1,2)$ and $(4,11)$.

questions.solution:
The dot product is the sum of the products of corresponding components:

$\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = (2)(1) + (3)(-1) + (1)(4)$

$= 2 - 3 + 4 = \mathbf{3}$.

questions.q: Find the radius of the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-8y = 0$.
questions.solution:
Here $2g=-6$ so $g=-3$; $2f=-8$ so $f=-4$; and $c=0$.

$r = \sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}-c} = \sqrt{9+16-0} = \sqrt{25} = \mathbf{5}$.

Since $c = 0$, the circle passes through the origin — as substituting $(0,0)$ confirms.

questions.q: Find the distance of the point $(3,4)$ from the line $3x+4y-10=0$.

Define the scalar and vector products of two vectors. Compare them in terms of the nature of the result, their geometric meaning, and their behaviour under a change of order. Give one physical application of each, and explain what each becomes when the vectors are parallel and when they are perpendicular.
questions.solution:
**The scalar (dot) product.**

$\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$

In components, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3$.

**The vector (cross) product.**

$\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta\;\hat{n}$

where $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector perpendicular to both, in the sense given by the right-hand rule. In components it is the determinant

$\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}$

**Comparison.**

**Nature of the result.** The dot product is a **scalar**, a single number with no direction. The cross product is a **vector**, with both magnitude and direction. This is the most important difference and the source of most errors: writing $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$ as a vector, or $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ as a number, is a category mistake.

The cross product is also only defined in three dimensions, whereas the dot product works in any number.

**Geometric meaning.** The dot product measures how much the two vectors point **along** each other — it is the projection of one onto the other, times the other's length. The cross product measures how much they point **across** each other, its magnitude being the **area of the parallelogram** they span.

So they are complementary: one extracts $\cos\theta$ and the other $\sin\theta$, and $(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^{2} + |\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^{2} = |\vec{a}|^{2}|\vec{b}|^{2}$.

**Order.** The dot product is **commutative**: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}$, since $\cos\theta$ does not care about order.

The cross product is **anticommutative**: $\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = -\vec{b}\times\vec{a}$. Reversing the order reverses the right-hand rule and so flips the direction. This is why the order in $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$ must be remembered.

**Physical applications.**

**Dot product: work.** $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d}$. Only the component of force along the displacement does work, which is exactly what the dot product extracts. It also explains why a centripetal force does no work: it is perpendicular to the motion, so the dot product is zero.

**Cross product: torque.** $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$. Only the component of force perpendicular to the position vector turns the body, which is what the cross product extracts — and the result is itself a vector along the axis of rotation. The magnetic force $\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ and angular momentum $\vec{L} = \vec{r}\times\vec{p}$ are the other two standard examples.

**The two special cases.**

**Parallel vectors** ($\theta = 0$): $\cos 0 = 1$ and $\sin 0 = 0$.

$\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|$ — the **maximum** possible.

$\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = \vec{0}$ — the parallelogram is degenerate and has no area.

In particular $\vec{a}\times\vec{a} = \vec{0}$ for every vector, which is why a force applied along the line to the pivot produces no torque.

**Perpendicular vectors** ($\theta = 90^\circ$): $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ and $\sin 90^\circ = 1$.

$\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0$ — the **minimum** in magnitude.

$|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}| = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|$ — the **maximum**, since the parallelogram is now a rectangle.

So the two products are extremal in opposite situations, which is precisely why they are used as tests: a vanishing **dot** product means perpendicular, and a vanishing **cross** product means parallel.
